interactions.label: A post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC ratio below 0.70 can overcall COPD in elderly pat

params.question: A post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC ratio below 0.70 can overcall COPD in elderly patients because the ratio naturally declines with age.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This statement is true. The FEV1/FVC ratio declines naturally with age, so the fixed 0.70 cut-off can overdiagnose COPD in elderly patients. Age-adjusted lower limits of normal are more reliable in this group — an important limitation to remember when interpreting spirometry.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct. The FEV1/FVC ratio falls physiologically with ageing, so the fixed GOLD threshold of 0.70 can misclassify healthy elderly individuals as having COPD. The lower limit of normal adjusted for age, sex, and height is more accurate in older patients.

interactions.label: A 55-year-old man presents with breathlessness that has worsened over three year

params.question: A 55-year-old man presents with breathlessness that has worsened over three years, daily grey sputum, and a 30-pack-year smoking history. Which historical pattern best distinguishes this as COPD rather than asthma?

answers.text: Breathlessness that is worse at night and improves by morning

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Nocturnal worsening with morning improvement is characteristic of asthma, where airway tone fluctuates with circadian rhythm — not of COPD's relentless course.

answers.text: Complete resolution of symptoms between episodes with identifiable triggers

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Full inter-episode recovery with clear triggers such as dust, cold air, or exercise is the hallmark of asthma's episodic, reversible nature.

answers.text: Progressive dyspnoea that never fully clears, with chronic sputum production

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. COPD is defined by relentless progression — breathlessness that never fully remits, chronic daily sputum, and a background of tobacco or biomass exposure. This irreversible, worsening pattern is the key historical distinction from asthma.

answers.text: Seasonal variation in wheeze with a family history of eczema and allergic rhinitis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Seasonal variability and an atopic background (eczema, rhinitis, family history of allergy) strongly favour asthma, not COPD.

overallFeedback.feedback: The key is that COPD never fully remits. Progressive breathlessness that worsens year on year, with daily sputum and a smoking or biomass history, is the hallmark — unlike asthma, where symptoms clear completely between episodes.
Well done. The contrast between asthma's episodic reversibility and COPD's relentless progression is the single most important distinction on history.

interactions.label: A 58-year-old smoker has a post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.62 and an FEV

params.question: A 58-year-old smoker has a post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.62 and an FEV1 of 45% of predicted. What is the GOLD stage of his COPD?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: GOLD 1 requires FEV1 ≥80% of predicted. This patient's FEV1 of 45% is far below that threshold.
GOLD 2 applies when FEV1 is 50–79% of predicted. At 45%, this patient falls just below the GOLD 2 range.
Correct. GOLD 3 (severe) applies when FEV1 is 30–49% of predicted. This patient's FEV1 of 45% places him squarely in GOLD stage 3, confirming severe airflow limitation.
GOLD 4 requires FEV1 below 30% of predicted. This patient's 45% is well above that cut-off.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember: GOLD staging uses FEV1 percentage of predicted after confirming obstruction. The thresholds are ≥80% (stage 1), 50–79% (stage 2), 30–49% (stage 3), and <30% (stage 4). At 45%, this patient is GOLD 3 — severe.

Correct. Once obstruction is confirmed (post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC <0.70), GOLD severity is staged by FEV1 as a percentage of predicted: ≥80 is stage 1, 50–79 is stage 2, 30–49 is stage 3, and <30 is stage 4.

interactions.label: According to the 2023 GINA guidelines, what is the recommended reliever for a ne

params.question: According to the 2023 GINA guidelines, what is the recommended reliever for a newly diagnosed asthmatic at Step 1?

answers.text: Salbutamol alone via metered-dose inhaler as needed

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The 2023 GINA guidelines specifically removed SABA-only as a recommended option at any step, because it relieves bronchospasm without addressing underlying airway inflammation.

answers.text: Low-dose inhaled corticosteroid plus formoterol as needed

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. GINA 2023 shifted the paradigm: from Step 1, the preferred reliever is low-dose ICS-formoterol, so every rescue dose simultaneously treats inflammation. This replaced the long-standing SABA-only approach.

answers.text: Daily oral montelukast with salbutamol for rescue

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Montelukast is an add-on controller useful in aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease and exercise-induced asthma. It is not the Step 1 reliever recommendation.
Tiotropium is an anticholinergic bronchodilator used primarily in COPD or as add-on therapy in refractory asthma at higher steps, not as a Step 1 reliever.

overallFeedback.feedback: The 2023 GINA paradigm shift is crucial: SABA-only is no longer recommended at any step. From Step 1, the preferred reliever is low-dose ICS-formoterol as needed, ensuring every rescue dose also treats the underlying inflammation.
Correct. The key paradigm shift is that every rescue dose now delivers an anti-inflammatory component, eliminating the risk of undertreated airway inflammation when patients rely on relievers alone.

interactions.label: A 50-year-old bidi smoker with COPD says he has been 'thinking about quitting bu

params.question: A 50-year-old bidi smoker with COPD says he has been 'thinking about quitting but is not ready yet.' Using the 5As framework, what is the most appropriate next step?

answers.text: Set a quit date immediately and prescribe nicotine replacement therapy

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Jumping to a quit date and pharmacotherapy skips the Assess step. A patient in the contemplation stage is not yet ready for a quit date — forcing one risks poor adherence and early relapse.

answers.text: Assess his readiness to quit and assist with a plan when he is prepared

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. After Ask and Advise, the next step is Assess — determine the patient's readiness using the Prochaska stages. This patient is in the contemplation stage. Assist with planning when he moves to preparation, and arrange follow-up within one to two weeks.

answers.text: Refer directly to a de-addiction centre without further discussion

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Referral without assessing readiness or providing brief counselling bypasses the framework. Empathetic engagement at the point of care is essential — relapse is the norm, and support works better than delegation alone.

answers.text: Document his refusal and revisit at the next annual check-up

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Waiting a full year misses the window for ongoing support. The 5As call for arranging follow-up within one to two weeks, maintaining momentum even when the patient is not yet ready to commit.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember the 5As: Ask about tobacco use, Advise clearly to quit, Assess readiness (this patient is in the contemplation stage), Assist with a plan when ready, and Arrange follow-up within one to two weeks. Empathy and non-judgmental support work better than blame.

Well done. The 5As — Ask, Advise, Assess, Assist, Arrange — are sequential for good reason. Matching your intervention to the patient's readiness stage improves quit rates and preserves the therapeutic relationship.
